chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Food, clothes, medicines, books and most things we use are based on the versatile element CARBON.
All living structures are carbon based.
The amount of carbon in nature is quite small: the earth's crust has only 0.02% carbon (in the form of minerals like carbonates, hydrogen-carbonates, coal and petroleum).
The atmosphere has 0.03% of CARBON DIOXIDE.
In spite of this small amount available in nature, the importance of carbon is immense.
The chapter studies the properties of carbon which make it so important to us.

chapter_sections.aim: To identify how many everyday items are made of compounds of carbon.
procedure: 1. Make a list of ten things you have used or consumed since the morning.
2. Compile this list with the lists made by your classmates and sort the items into a table with columns - Things made of metal, Things made of glass/clay, Others.
3. If there are items made up of more than one material, put them into both the relevant columns of the table.
chapter_sections.observation: The items in the last column ("Others") are mostly made up of compounds of carbon.

topics.topic_name: BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: IONIC COMPOUNDS have high melting and boiling points and conduct electricity in solution or in the molten state.
Most CARBON COMPOUNDS are poor conductors of electricity and have low melting and boiling points compared to ionic compounds.
This shows the forces of attraction between molecules of carbon compounds are not very strong, and the bonding does NOT give rise to ions.
The COMBINING CAPACITY (valency) of an element depends on the number of valence electrons.
The atomic number of CARBON is 6; it has FOUR valence electrons (TETRAVALENT).
Reactivity is explained as the tendency of atoms to attain a completely filled outer shell (noble gas configuration).
Carbon needs to gain or lose four electrons to attain noble gas configuration, but:
(i) Gaining 4 electrons (forming C4- anion) is difficult, as the nucleus with six protons cannot hold ten electrons.
(ii) Losing 4 electrons (forming C4+ cation) requires a large amount of energy.
Carbon overcomes this by SHARING its four valence electrons with other atoms - forming COVALENT BONDS.
SINGLE BOND: one shared pair of electrons (e.g. H2, represented as H - H).
DOUBLE BOND: two shared pairs of electrons (e.g. O2, represented as O = O).
TRIPLE BOND: three shared pairs of electrons (e.g. N2, represented as N (triple bond) N).

Examples of covalent molecules: Hydrogen (H2 - single bond), Chlorine (Cl2 - single bond), Oxygen (O2 - double bond), Nitrogen (N2 - triple bond), Ammonia (NH3), Water (H2O), Methane (CH4 - four single bonds, carbon shares its 4 electrons with 4 hydrogen atoms).
Covalently bonded molecules have STRONG bonds within the molecule, but WEAK intermolecular forces - giving low melting and boiling points.
Since electrons are shared and no charged particles are formed, covalent compounds are generally POOR CONDUCTORS of electricity.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (More to Know - Allotropes of carbon):
sections.text:
- The element carbon occurs in different forms (ALLOTROPES) in nature with widely varying physical properties.
- DIAMOND: each carbon atom is bonded to FOUR other carbon atoms forming a rigid three-dimensional structure. Diamond is the HARDEST substance known.
- GRAPHITE: each carbon atom is bonded to THREE other carbon atoms in the same plane giving a hexagonal array; one bond is a double bond so valency is satisfied. Structure is hexagonal arrays placed in layers one above the other. Graphite is SMOOTH, SLIPPERY and a very good CONDUCTOR of electricity (unlike other non-metals).
- Diamond and graphite have very different physical properties but the SAME chemical properties.
- Diamonds can be SYNTHESISED by subjecting pure carbon to very high pressure and temperature; synthetic diamonds are small but otherwise indistinguishable from natural diamonds.
- FULLERENES form another class of carbon allotropes. The first identified was C-60 (sixty carbon atoms arranged in the shape of a football). It was named FULLERENE after the geodesic dome designed by US architect Buckminster Fuller (C-60 Buckminsterfullerene).

items.question: What would be the electron dot structure of carbon dioxide which has the formula CO2?
items.answer: In CO2, the carbon atom forms TWO double bonds, one with each oxygen atom (O = C = O). Carbon shares two of its electrons with each oxygen (two shared pairs per oxygen). The structure: each oxygen has two lone pairs and shares two pairs with carbon, so carbon completes its octet (8 electrons) and each oxygen completes its octet. Represented with dots/crosses: O::C::O.

items.question: What would be the electron dot structure of a molecule of sulphur which is made up of eight atoms of sulphur? (Hint: The eight atoms of sulphur are joined together in the form of a ring.)
items.answer:
In S8, the eight sulphur atoms are joined in a RING. Each sulphur atom forms TWO single covalent bonds with two neighbouring sulphur atoms (each sharing one electron pair). Each sulphur has two lone pairs and two bonding pairs, completing its octet. The structure is a closed eight-membered ring (S - S - S - S - S - S - S - S joined end to end).

items.question: What is a covalent bond? Give one example.
items.answer: A COVALENT BOND is a bond formed by the SHARING of an electron pair between two atoms. The shared electrons belong to the outermost shells of both atoms and help both achieve the noble gas configuration. Example: In a hydrogen molecule (H2), the two hydrogen atoms share one pair of electrons forming a single covalent bond (H - H).

items.question: Why is carbon said to be tetravalent?
items.answer: The atomic number of carbon is 6, so it has FOUR electrons in its outermost (valence) shell. To attain a stable noble gas configuration it needs to share these four electrons by forming four bonds. Because it has four valence electrons and forms four bonds, carbon is said to be TETRAVALENT.

items.question: Distinguish between single, double and triple covalent bonds with one example each.
items.answer:
- SINGLE BOND: one shared pair of electrons between two atoms. Example: Hydrogen molecule, H - H.
- DOUBLE BOND: two shared pairs of electrons between two atoms. Example: Oxygen molecule, O = O.
- TRIPLE BOND: three shared pairs of electrons between two atoms. Example: Nitrogen molecule, N (triple bond) N.

items.question: Why can carbon neither gain nor lose four electrons easily? How does it overcome this?
items.answer:
Carbon has four valence electrons and needs to gain or lose four electrons to attain noble gas configuration.
(i) It cannot easily GAIN four electrons (forming C4-) because the nucleus with only six protons cannot hold on to ten electrons (four extra electrons).
(ii) It cannot easily LOSE four electrons (forming C4+) because a large amount of energy would be required to remove four electrons, leaving a cation with six protons holding only two electrons.
Carbon OVERCOMES this problem by SHARING its valence electrons with other atoms of carbon or other elements, thereby forming COVALENT BONDS and attaining a stable noble gas configuration.

items.question: Compare the properties of ionic compounds and covalent compounds with respect to melting/boiling points and electrical conductivity.
items.answer:
IONIC COMPOUNDS:
- Have HIGH melting and boiling points (strong forces of attraction between ions).
- CONDUCT electricity in solution or in the molten state (due to free-moving ions).
COVALENT COMPOUNDS (carbon compounds):
- Have LOW melting and boiling points (weak intermolecular forces, though strong bonds within the molecule).
- Are generally POOR conductors of electricity (electrons are shared, no charged particles/ions are formed).

items.question: Explain the formation of covalent bonds in hydrogen (H2), oxygen (O2), nitrogen (N2) and methane (CH4) using the concept of electron sharing.
items.answer:
HYDROGEN (H2): Atomic number of hydrogen is 1, so it has one electron in its K shell and needs one more to fill it. Two hydrogen atoms share their electrons (one shared pair) to form a SINGLE covalent bond (H - H), each attaining the configuration of helium.
OXYGEN (O2): Atomic number of oxygen is 8, with six electrons in its L shell; it needs two more to complete its octet. Each oxygen atom shares two electrons with the other (two shared pairs), forming a DOUBLE bond (O = O).
NITROGEN (N2): Atomic number of nitrogen is 7. To attain an octet, each nitrogen contributes three electrons giving three shared pairs, forming a TRIPLE bond (N (triple bond) N).
METHANE (CH4): Carbon is tetravalent (four valence electrons) and hydrogen has a valency of 1. Carbon shares its four electrons with four hydrogen atoms, forming four single covalent bonds. Each hydrogen attains the helium configuration and carbon completes its octet.

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: DEFINITION: The VERSATILE NATURE OF CARBON refers to carbon's unique ability to form a very large number of compounds (millions) due to two factors - CATENATION (the ability to form bonds with other carbon atoms giving long chains, branches and rings) and TETRAVALENCY (the ability to bond with four other atoms of carbon or other elements).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The number of carbon compounds known to chemists is in MILLIONS - more than the compounds of all other elements put together.
Two factors responsible for carbon forming so many compounds:

(i) CATENATION: Carbon has the unique ability to form bonds with other atoms of carbon, giving large molecules. These may be long chains, branched chains, or rings. Carbon atoms may be linked by single, double or triple bonds.
SATURATED COMPOUNDS: carbon compounds linked by ONLY SINGLE bonds.
UNSATURATED COMPOUNDS: carbon compounds having DOUBLE or TRIPLE bonds between carbon atoms.

No other element shows catenation to the extent of carbon. Silicon forms compounds with hydrogen having chains up to seven or eight atoms, but these are very reactive. The carbon-carbon bond is very strong and stable.

(ii) TETRAVALENCY: Since carbon has a valency of four, it can bond with four other carbon atoms or atoms of other monovalent elements. Carbon forms compounds with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine etc.

Bonds carbon forms with most other elements are very STRONG, making the compounds exceptionally stable. The reason is carbon's SMALL SIZE - the nucleus can hold the shared electron pairs strongly. Bonds formed by elements with bigger atoms are much weaker.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (More to Know - Organic compounds):
sections.text:
- The two characteristic features of carbon (TETRAVALENCY and CATENATION) give rise to a large number of compounds.
- These were initially extracted from natural substances; it was thought such carbon (ORGANIC) compounds could only be formed within a living system (a "vital force" was thought necessary).
- Friedrich Wohler DISPROVED this in 1828 by preparing UREA from ammonium cyanate.
- Carbon compounds (except carbides, oxides of carbon, carbonate and hydrogencarbonate salts) continue to be studied under organic chemistry.

items.question: What is catenation?
items.answer: CATENATION is the unique ability of carbon to form bonds with other atoms of carbon, giving rise to large molecules. These may be long straight chains, branched chains, or rings linked by single, double or triple bonds.

items.question: Define saturated and unsaturated carbon compounds.
items.answer: SATURATED compounds are carbon compounds in which carbon atoms are linked by ONLY SINGLE bonds. UNSATURATED compounds are carbon compounds having DOUBLE or TRIPLE bonds between their carbon atoms.

items.question: Name the two factors that make carbon form a very large number of compounds and explain each briefly.
items.answer:
(i) CATENATION: Carbon can form strong bonds with other carbon atoms, giving long chains, branched chains and rings (single, double or triple bonds). This gives a huge number of compounds.
(ii) TETRAVALENCY: Carbon has a valency of four, so it can bond with four other carbon atoms or atoms of other monovalent elements (oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine, etc.), giving compounds with varied properties.

items.question: Why does carbon form a larger number of compounds than silicon, even though both show catenation?
items.answer: Although silicon also shows catenation, it forms compounds with hydrogen having chains of only up to seven or eight atoms, and these compounds are VERY REACTIVE (unstable). Carbon, on the other hand, forms very STRONG and STABLE carbon-carbon bonds because of its SMALL atomic size - the nucleus holds the shared electrons strongly. This stability allows carbon to form a much larger number of compounds with many carbon atoms linked together, far more than silicon.

items.question: How did Friedrich Wohler change the understanding of organic compounds?
items.answer: Earlier it was believed that organic (carbon) compounds could only be formed inside a living system, with the help of a "vital force". In 1828, Friedrich Wohler DISPROVED this belief by preparing UREA (an organic compound) from ammonium cyanate (an inorganic source) in the laboratory. This showed organic compounds can be made artificially without any vital force. Today, carbon compounds (except carbides, oxides of carbon, carbonates and hydrogencarbonates) are studied under organic chemistry.

items.question: Explain how the tetravalency and small size of carbon together account for the versatile nature of carbon.
items.answer:
TETRAVALENCY: Carbon has four valence electrons and a valency of four. This allows it to form four covalent bonds - either with four carbon atoms or with atoms of other elements such as oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur and chlorine. Hence carbon can build a wide variety of compounds with different elements.
CATENATION (linked to small size): Carbon can bond with other carbon atoms to form long chains, branched chains and rings. The bonds carbon forms are very STRONG and STABLE.
SMALL SIZE: Because the carbon atom is small, its nucleus can hold the shared pairs of electrons tightly, making the bonds strong. Elements with larger atoms form weaker bonds.
Together, tetravalency (variety of partners) and small size (strong, stable bonds enabling catenation) explain why carbon forms millions of compounds - more than all other elements combined - making it a versatile element.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: METHANE (CH4): simplest carbon compound, all single bonds.
ETHANE (C2H6): formed between carbon and hydrogen. Structure arrived in steps:
Step 1: Link the carbon atoms with a single bond (C - C).
Step 2: Three valencies of each carbon remain unsatisfied, so each is bonded to three hydrogen atoms (H3C - CH3).
PROPANE (C3H8): all valencies satisfied by single bonds (a saturated compound).
Saturated compounds (single bonds only) are normally NOT very reactive.
ETHENE (C2H4): one valency per carbon remains unsatisfied with single bonds; satisfied only by a DOUBLE bond between the two carbons (C = C). It is an UNSATURATED compound.
ETHYNE (C2H2): requires a TRIPLE bond between the two carbon atoms to satisfy their valencies. It is UNSATURATED.
Unsaturated carbon compounds (with double or triple bonds) are MORE REACTIVE than saturated compounds.

items.question: Write the molecular formulae of ethane, ethene and ethyne.
items.answer: Ethane = C2H6 (saturated, single bond), Ethene = C2H4 (unsaturated, double bond), Ethyne = C2H2 (unsaturated, triple bond).

items.question: Why are unsaturated compounds more reactive than saturated compounds?
items.answer: Unsaturated compounds contain double or triple bonds between carbon atoms. These multiple bonds are reactive sites that can take part in reactions (such as addition reactions), making unsaturated compounds MORE reactive. Saturated compounds have only single bonds and are normally not very reactive.

items.question: Describe the steps to arrive at the structure of ethane (C2H6).
items.answer:
Step 1: Link the two carbon atoms together with a SINGLE bond (C - C).
Step 2: After linking, three valencies of each carbon remain unsatisfied. So each carbon atom is bonded to THREE hydrogen atoms.
Result: The structure is H3C - CH3, with each carbon having four bonds (one to carbon, three to hydrogen). Ethane is a saturated compound.

items.question: Explain why ethene contains a double bond, with the steps used to arrive at its structure.
items.answer:
Ethene has the formula C2H4.
Step 1: The two carbon atoms are linked together with a single bond (C - C).
Step 2: With single bonds, ONE valency per carbon atom remains unsatisfied.
Step 3: This unsatisfied valency can be satisfied only if there is a DOUBLE bond between the two carbon atoms (C = C).
Hence ethene has a carbon-carbon double bond and is an unsaturated compound.

items.question: Differentiate between saturated and unsaturated carbon compounds with examples.
items.answer:
SATURATED CARBON COMPOUNDS:
- Contain only SINGLE bonds between carbon atoms.
- Normally NOT very reactive.
- Examples: methane (CH4), ethane (C2H6), propane (C3H8).
UNSATURATED CARBON COMPOUNDS:
- Contain DOUBLE or TRIPLE bonds between carbon atoms.
- MORE reactive than saturated compounds.
- Examples: ethene (C2H4, double bond), ethyne (C2H2, triple bond).

items.question: Starting from carbon-carbon linking, explain how the structures of ethane, ethene and ethyne are built up.
items.answer:
ETHANE (C2H6):
Step 1: Join two carbon atoms with a single bond (C - C).
Step 2: Three valencies on each carbon remain free, satisfied by three hydrogen atoms each, giving H3C - CH3. All single bonds - saturated.
ETHENE (C2H4):
Step 1: Join two carbons with a single bond (C - C).
Step 2: One valency per carbon remains unsatisfied.
Step 3: Satisfied by a DOUBLE bond between the carbons (C = C), with two hydrogen atoms on each carbon. Unsaturated.
ETHYNE (C2H2):
The two carbon atoms need a TRIPLE bond to satisfy their valencies, with one hydrogen on each carbon (H - C (triple bond) C - H). Unsaturated and more reactive.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Chains of carbon atoms can contain many carbon atoms (methane = 1C, ethane = 2C, propane = 3C, and so on).

STRUCTURAL ISOMERS: compounds with identical molecular formula but different structures. Example: butane (C4H10) has two possible carbon skeletons (straight chain and branched), giving two structural isomers.
CYCLIC (RING) compounds: carbon atoms arranged in the form of a ring. Example: CYCLOHEXANE (C6H12).
BENZENE (C6H6): a cyclic compound; an example of an unsaturated cyclic hydrocarbon.
Straight chain, branched chain and cyclic carbon compounds may all be saturated or unsaturated.
HYDROCARBONS: compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen.
ALKANES: saturated hydrocarbons (only single bonds).
ALKENES: unsaturated hydrocarbons containing one or more DOUBLE bonds.
ALKYNES: unsaturated hydrocarbons containing one or more TRIPLE bonds.

items.question: What are structural isomers? Give an example.
items.answer: Compounds with the SAME molecular formula but DIFFERENT structures are called STRUCTURAL ISOMERS. Example: butane (C4H10) exists as a straight-chain isomer and a branched-chain isomer.

items.question: Define hydrocarbons and name their three classes.
items.answer: HYDROCARBONS are carbon compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen. The three classes are ALKANES (saturated), ALKENES (with double bonds) and ALKYNES (with triple bonds).

items.question: Write the names and formulae of the first three saturated hydrocarbons.
items.answer:
1 carbon: Methane - CH4
2 carbons: Ethane - C2H6
3 carbons: Propane - C3H8
(These are saturated compounds with only single bonds.)

items.question: Distinguish between alkanes, alkenes and alkynes with one example each.
items.answer:
- ALKANES: saturated hydrocarbons containing only single bonds. Example: methane (CH4), ethane (C2H6).
- ALKENES: unsaturated hydrocarbons containing one or more DOUBLE bonds. Example: ethene (C2H4).
- ALKYNES: unsaturated hydrocarbons containing one or more TRIPLE bonds. Example: ethyne (C2H2).

items.question: What is meant by a cyclic compound? Give two examples and state whether they are saturated or unsaturated.
items.answer:
A CYCLIC (RING) compound is one in which the carbon atoms are arranged in the form of a ring rather than a chain.
Examples:
- CYCLOHEXANE (C6H12) - a saturated cyclic compound.
- BENZENE (C6H6) - an unsaturated cyclic compound.
Cyclic compounds may thus be either saturated or unsaturated.

items.question: Explain straight chains, branched chains and rings of carbon, and how structural isomers arise, using butane as an example.
items.answer:
STRAIGHT CHAINS: Carbon atoms link one after another in a line (e.g. butane straight chain: C - C - C - C).
BRANCHED CHAINS: A carbon chain that has a branch (side group), e.g. the branched skeleton of butane.
RINGS: Carbon atoms arranged in a closed ring, e.g. cyclohexane (C6H12).
STRUCTURAL ISOMERS: For butane (C4H10), two different carbon skeletons are possible - a straight four-carbon chain and a branched chain. Both have the same molecular formula C4H10 but different structures. Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are called structural isomers. Filling the remaining valencies with hydrogen gives the two complete isomeric molecules of butane.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Carbon also bonds with elements such as halogens, oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur.
In a hydrocarbon chain, one or more hydrogens can be REPLACED by these elements so that carbon's valency is still satisfied.
The element replacing hydrogen is called a HETEROATOM.
FUNCTIONAL GROUPS: heteroatoms and the groups containing them confer specific properties to the compound, regardless of the length and nature of the carbon chain.
The free valency (or valencies) of the group is shown by a single line; the functional group attaches to the carbon chain through this valency, replacing a hydrogen atom.

items.question: What is a heteroatom? Give two examples.
items.answer: A HETEROATOM is an atom that replaces one or more hydrogen atoms in a hydrocarbon chain while keeping carbon's valency satisfied. Examples: chlorine (Cl), oxygen (O), bromine (Br), nitrogen (N), sulphur (S).

items.question: What is a functional group? Name the functional groups of alcohols, aldehydes and carboxylic acids.
items.answer:
A FUNCTIONAL GROUP is a heteroatom or a group containing a heteroatom that confers specific properties to a compound, regardless of the length of the carbon chain.
- Alcohol: -OH
- Aldehyde: -CHO
- Carboxylic acid: -COOH

items.question: List the classes of compounds for the functional groups -Cl/-Br, -OH, -CO- and -COOH, with their characteristic group.
items.answer:
- -Cl, -Br : Halo (chloro/bromo) alkane (halogen substitutes for a hydrogen atom).
- -OH : Alcohol.
- -CO- (carbon double-bonded to oxygen, between two carbons): Ketone.
- -COOH : Carboxylic acid.
(The aldehyde group -CHO, with carbon double-bonded to oxygen and bonded to hydrogen, also contains oxygen as the heteroatom.)

options.C: regardless of the length of the carbon chain

items.explanation: The functional group decides chemical properties irrespective of chain length, which is why a homologous series shares properties.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The presence of a functional group (e.g. alcohol) decides the properties of the compound, regardless of the length of the carbon chain.
Example: CH3OH, C2H5OH, C3H7OH and C4H9OH all have very similar chemical properties (all are alcohols).
In a homologous series, successive compounds differ by a -CH2- unit.
CH4 and C2H6 differ by a -CH2- unit.
C2H6 and C3H8 differ by a -CH2- unit.
The difference in molecular mass between successive members is 14 u (atomic mass of C = 12 u, of H = 1 u; -CH2- = 12 + 2 = 14 u).
ALKENE general formula: CnH2n (n = 2, 3, 4...). First member is ETHENE.
ALKANE general formula: CnH2n+2.
ALKYNE general formula: CnH2n-2.

As molecular mass increases in a homologous series, a gradation in PHYSICAL properties is seen: melting and boiling points increase with increasing molecular mass; solubility in a particular solvent also shows gradation.
CHEMICAL properties (determined by the functional group) remain SIMILAR within a homologous series.

items.question: Define a homologous series.
items.answer: A HOMOLOGOUS SERIES is a series of compounds in which the same functional group substitutes for hydrogen in a carbon chain, and where successive members differ from each other by a -CH2- unit.

items.question: By what unit and molecular mass do successive members of a homologous series differ?
items.answer: Successive members differ by a -CH2- unit, which corresponds to a difference in molecular mass of 14 u (carbon = 12 u + two hydrogen = 2 u).

items.question: Write the general formulae of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
items.answer:
- Alkanes: CnH2n+2
- Alkenes: CnH2n
- Alkynes: CnH2n-2
(where n is the number of carbon atoms.)

items.question: Why do members of a homologous series have similar chemical properties but show a gradation in physical properties?
items.answer: All members of a homologous series contain the SAME functional group, and chemical properties are determined solely by the functional group. Hence their chemical properties remain SIMILAR. However, as the carbon chain lengthens, the molecular mass increases. Physical properties such as melting point, boiling point and solubility depend on molecular mass, so they show a gradual change (GRADATION) along the series.

items.question: Show that the alcohols CH3OH, C2H5OH, C3H7OH form a homologous series.
items.answer:
- CH3OH and C2H5OH differ by a -CH2- unit (difference in molecular mass = 14 u).
- C2H5OH and C3H7OH differ by a -CH2- unit (difference in molecular mass = 14 u).
All three contain the same functional group -OH (alcohol), and successive members differ by -CH2-. Hence they form a HOMOLOGOUS SERIES (the alcohol family) with similar chemical properties.

items.question: Explain the features of a homologous series with reference to the alkanes.
items.answer:
A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group, where successive members differ by -CH2- (molecular mass difference 14 u). For the ALKANES (general formula CnH2n+2):
- CH4 (methane), C2H6 (ethane), C3H8 (propane), C4H10 (butane)...
- Each successive member differs from the previous by a -CH2- unit (e.g. CH4 to C2H6, C2H6 to C3H8).
- The difference in molecular mass between successive members is 14 u.
- CHEMICAL properties remain similar (all are saturated, relatively unreactive hydrocarbons).
- PHYSICAL properties (melting point, boiling point, solubility) show a gradation, increasing with molecular mass.

points: The names of compounds in a homologous series are based on the name of the basic carbon chain, modified by a PREFIX or SUFFIX indicating the functional group.
RULES for naming a carbon compound:
(i) Identify the NUMBER of carbon atoms in the compound (e.g. three carbons -> "propane").
(ii) If a functional group is present, it is indicated by a PREFIX or SUFFIX (as given in Table 4.4).

(iii) If the functional group's suffix begins with a vowel (a, e, i, o, u), the final 'e' of the carbon chain name is deleted before adding the suffix. Example: a three-carbon chain with a ketone group -> propane - 'e' + 'one' = PROPANONE.

(iv) If the carbon chain is unsaturated, the final 'ane' is replaced by 'ene' (double bond) or 'yne' (triple bond). Example: three-carbon chain with a double bond = PROPENE; with a triple bond = PROPYNE.
TABLE 4.4 - NOMENCLATURE OF ORGANIC COMPOUNDS:
Class of compounds | Prefix/Suffix          | Example (3 carbons)
1. Halo alkane     | Prefix - chloro, bromo | Chloropropane / Bromopropane
2. Alcohol         | Suffix - ol            | Propanol
3. Aldehyde        | Suffix - al            | Propanal
4. Ketone          | Suffix - one           | Propanone
5. Carboxylic acid | Suffix - oic acid      | Propanoic acid
6. Alkenes         | Suffix - ene           | Propene
7. Alkynes         | Suffix - yne           | Propyne

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: DEFINITION: The CHEMICAL PROPERTIES of carbon compounds include the important reactions they undergo - combustion, oxidation, addition reactions and substitution reactions. Since most fuels are carbon or its compounds, combustion is studied first.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Most fuels we use are either carbon or its compounds.
The main chemical reactions of carbon compounds studied are: COMBUSTION, OXIDATION, ADDITION reactions, and SUBSTITUTION reactions.

items.question: Name the four main chemical reactions of carbon compounds.
items.answer: The four main reactions are COMBUSTION, OXIDATION, ADDITION reactions and SUBSTITUTION reactions.

items.question: Why is combustion studied first among the chemical properties of carbon compounds?
items.answer: Because most of the fuels we use are either carbon or carbon compounds, and combustion (burning in oxygen) is the reaction by which these fuels release energy, it is the most important and is studied first.

items.question: What is an oxidising agent? Give two examples used to oxidise alcohols.
items.answer: An OXIDISING AGENT is a substance capable of adding oxygen to others. Two examples used to oxidise alcohols to carboxylic acids are alkaline POTASSIUM PERMANGANATE and acidified POTASSIUM DICHROMATE.

items.question: Distinguish between addition reactions and substitution reactions.
items.answer:
ADDITION REACTION: Unsaturated hydrocarbons ADD hydrogen (or other atoms) in the presence of catalysts (e.g. palladium, nickel) to give saturated hydrocarbons. It is typical of unsaturated compounds.
SUBSTITUTION REACTION: One type of atom or group of atoms takes the PLACE of another (e.g. chlorine replaces hydrogen atoms in saturated hydrocarbons in sunlight). It is typical of saturated hydrocarbons.

items.question: Write the combustion reactions (word/equation) for carbon, methane and ethanol.
items.answer:
- Carbon: C + O2 -> CO2 + heat and light
- Methane: CH4 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O + heat and light
- Ethanol: CH3CH2OH + O2 -> CO2 + H2O + heat and light
(The latter two need to be balanced; they release heat and light as oxidation reactions.)

items.question: Explain combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions of carbon compounds, one line each with an example.
items.answer:
- COMBUSTION: Carbon and its compounds burn in oxygen to give carbon dioxide along with heat and light. Example: CH4 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O + heat and light.
- OXIDATION: Alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by oxidising agents. Example: ethanol -> ethanoic acid using alkaline KMnO4.
- ADDITION: Unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in the presence of nickel/palladium catalysts to give saturated hydrocarbons (hydrogenation of vegetable oils).
- SUBSTITUTION: In saturated hydrocarbons, an atom is replaced by another in sunlight. Example: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl (in the presence of sunlight).

items.question: Burning of carbon compounds in oxygen is called
items.explanation: Combustion is burning in oxygen producing CO2, heat and light. Addition and substitution are different reaction types.

items.question: Which reaction is characteristic of unsaturated hydrocarbons?
items.explanation: Unsaturated compounds undergo addition reactions (e.g. add hydrogen). Substitution is typical of saturated hydrocarbons.

items.question: A substance capable of adding oxygen to others is called a/an
items.explanation: An oxidising agent adds oxygen (e.g. KMnO4). A reducing agent removes oxygen / adds hydrogen.

items.question: The reaction CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl (in sunlight) is a
items.explanation: Chlorine replaces a hydrogen atom in methane, a substitution reaction occurring in sunlight.

items.question: Vegetable oils are converted to fats by adding hydrogen using a catalyst of
items.explanation: Hydrogenation of vegetable oils uses a nickel catalyst (also palladium). The other metals are not used here.

items.question: Acidified potassium dichromate acts as a/an ___ in the conversion of alcohol to acid.
items.explanation: Acidified K2Cr2O7 adds oxygen to convert alcohol to carboxylic acid, so it is an oxidising agent.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Carbon in all its allotropic forms burns in oxygen to give CARBON DIOXIDE along with heat and light.
Most carbon compounds also release a large amount of heat and light on burning.
Combustion reactions are OXIDATION reactions:
(i) C + O2 -> CO2 + heat and light
(ii) CH4 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O + heat and light
(iii) CH3CH2OH + O2 -> CO2 + H2O + heat and light
SATURATED hydrocarbons generally give a CLEAN (blue) flame.
UNSATURATED carbon compounds give a YELLOW flame with lots of black smoke (soot).
LIMITING the supply of air leads to INCOMPLETE COMBUSTION even of saturated hydrocarbons, giving a sooty flame.
Gas/kerosene stoves have inlets for air so a sufficiently oxygen-rich mixture is burnt to give a CLEAN BLUE flame.
Blackened bottoms of cooking vessels indicate the air holes are blocked and fuel is being wasted.
Coal and petroleum contain some nitrogen and sulphur; their combustion forms OXIDES OF SULPHUR AND NITROGEN, which are major air POLLUTANTS.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (Do you know? - Why do substances burn with or without a flame?):
sections.text:
- A FLAME is produced only when GASEOUS substances burn.
- When wood or charcoal is ignited, the volatile substances present vapourise and burn with a flame at the beginning; coal/charcoal in an "angithi" sometimes just glows red and gives heat without a flame.
- A LUMINOUS flame is seen when the atoms of the gaseous substance are heated and start to glow.
- The colour produced by each element is a characteristic property of that element (e.g. heat a copper wire in a flame and observe its colour).
- Incomplete combustion gives soot (carbon), which is the reason for the yellow colour of a candle flame.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (More to Know - Formation of coal and petroleum):
sections.text:
- COAL and PETROLEUM have been formed from biomass subjected to various biological and geological processes.
- COAL: the remains of trees, ferns and other plants that lived millions of years ago, crushed into the earth (by earthquakes/volcanic eruptions), pressed down by layers of earth and rock, slowly decaying into coal.
- OIL and GAS: the remains of millions of tiny plants and animals that lived in the sea; when they died, their bodies sank to the sea bed and were covered by silt. Bacteria turned the remains into oil and gas under high pressure; the silt was compressed into rock, and the oil/gas seeped into porous rock and got trapped.
- Coal and petroleum are called FOSSIL FUELS (formed from the fossilised remains of living things).

items.question: What is combustion? Write the combustion reaction of carbon.
items.answer: COMBUSTION is the burning of carbon and its compounds in oxygen to give carbon dioxide along with heat and light. Reaction of carbon: C + O2 -> CO2 + heat and light.

items.question: Why do saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean flame while unsaturated compounds give a sooty flame?
items.answer: Saturated hydrocarbons burn completely in sufficient oxygen, giving a clean (blue) flame. Unsaturated compounds have a higher proportion of carbon and do not burn completely, releasing unburnt carbon as black soot - a yellow sooty flame.

items.question: Why does a gas/kerosene stove give a clean blue flame, and what does a blackened vessel bottom indicate?
items.answer: A gas/kerosene stove has inlets for AIR so that a sufficiently OXYGEN-RICH mixture is burnt, giving complete combustion and a clean BLUE flame. If the bottom of a cooking vessel gets blackened, it means the air holes are BLOCKED, causing incomplete combustion (sooty flame) and fuel is being wasted.

items.question: How does limiting the air supply affect combustion? Why are coal and petroleum combustion harmful?
items.answer: LIMITING the air supply causes INCOMPLETE COMBUSTION even of saturated hydrocarbons, producing a sooty (yellow) flame and unburnt carbon. Coal and petroleum contain some NITROGEN and SULPHUR; their combustion produces OXIDES of sulphur and nitrogen, which are major air POLLUTANTS harmful to the environment.

items.question: Explain why a flame is produced only when gaseous substances burn, with the example of wood/charcoal.
items.answer: A FLAME is produced only when GASEOUS substances burn. When wood or charcoal is ignited, the VOLATILE substances present vapourise and burn with a flame in the beginning. Once these volatile substances are used up, the remaining charcoal (in an angithi) simply GLOWS red and gives heat WITHOUT a flame, because there is no gaseous substance left to burn with a flame.

items.question: Describe combustion of carbon compounds, types of flames, and the formation of fossil fuels.
items.answer:
COMBUSTION: Carbon and its compounds burn in oxygen to give CO2, water (for hydrocarbons) and heat and light (oxidation reactions).
TYPES OF FLAME: Saturated hydrocarbons give a CLEAN BLUE flame (complete combustion). Unsaturated compounds give a YELLOW SOOTY flame (incomplete combustion). Limited air gives a sooty flame even for saturated compounds. A flame forms only when gaseous substances burn.
FOSSIL FUELS: Coal is formed from the remains of trees, ferns and plants buried millions of years ago, pressed and decayed under earth and rock. Oil and gas are formed from the remains of tiny sea plants and animals, attacked by bacteria under high pressure, with silt compressed into rock and oil/gas trapped in porous rock. Hence coal and petroleum are called FOSSIL FUELS.

points: Carbon compounds can be easily oxidised on combustion (complete oxidation).
In addition, there are reactions in which ALCOHOLS are converted to CARBOXYLIC ACIDS.

(Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid.)
Substances capable of ADDING OXYGEN to others are called OXIDISING AGENTS.
Alkaline POTASSIUM PERMANGANATE (KMnO4) and acidified POTASSIUM DICHROMATE (K2Cr2O7) are oxidising agents - they add oxygen to the starting material (alcohol -> acid).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 4.5:
sections.aim: To observe the oxidation of ethanol by alkaline potassium permanganate.
sections.materials: About 3 mL ethanol, test tube, water bath, 5% solution of alkaline potassium permanganate.
procedure: 1. Take about 3 mL of ethanol in a test tube and warm it gently in a water bath.
2. Add a 5% solution of alkaline potassium permanganate drop by drop to this solution.
3. Observe whether the colour of potassium permanganate persists when it is added initially.
4. Observe why the colour does not disappear when excess is added.
sections.observation: Initially the purple colour of KMnO4 disappears (it is being used up to oxidise the ethanol). When excess KMnO4 is added, all the ethanol has been oxidised, so the colour persists.
sections.conclusion:
Alkaline potassium permanganate acts as an OXIDISING AGENT, oxidising ethanol to ethanoic acid. Once all the alcohol is oxidised, excess KMnO4 is not used up and its colour remains.

items.question: What is an oxidising agent? Name two oxidising agents that convert alcohols to acids.
items.answer: An OXIDISING AGENT is a substance capable of adding oxygen to others. Two oxidising agents that convert alcohols to acids are alkaline POTASSIUM PERMANGANATE (KMnO4) and acidified POTASSIUM DICHROMATE (K2Cr2O7).

items.question: Why is the conversion of ethanol to ethanoic acid called an oxidation reaction?
items.answer: In this reaction, OXYGEN is added to ethanol (an alcohol) to convert it into ethanoic acid (a carboxylic acid). Since addition of oxygen to a substance is oxidation, the conversion of ethanol to ethanoic acid is an OXIDATION reaction. The oxidising agent (alkaline KMnO4 or acidified K2Cr2O7) supplies the oxygen.

items.question: In Activity 4.5, why does the colour of potassium permanganate first disappear and later persist when excess is added?
items.answer:
Initially, when KMnO4 is added drop by drop to warm ethanol, the purple colour DISAPPEARS because the permanganate is being used up (reduced) as it oxidises the ethanol to ethanoic acid. As more is added, the ethanol continues to be oxidised. When EXCESS KMnO4 is added, ALL the ethanol has already been oxidised, so there is nothing left to react with; the permanganate is no longer used up and its purple colour PERSISTS.

points: Unsaturated hydrocarbons add HYDROGEN in the presence of CATALYSTS (palladium or nickel) to give SATURATED hydrocarbons.

items.question: Why are oils containing unsaturated fatty acids recommended for cooking over animal fats?
items.answer:
VEGETABLE OILS generally have long UNSATURATED carbon chains, while ANIMAL FATS generally contain SATURATED fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids are said to be HARMFUL for health. Therefore, oils containing UNSATURATED fatty acids (vegetable oils) are considered "healthy" and should be chosen for cooking, rather than animal fats which contain saturated fatty acids.

However, in the presence of SUNLIGHT, CHLORINE is added to hydrocarbons in a very FAST reaction.

items.question: What is a substitution reaction? Give one example.
items.answer: A SUBSTITUTION REACTION is a reaction in which one type of atom or group of atoms takes the PLACE of another. Example: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl (in the presence of sunlight), where chlorine replaces a hydrogen atom.

items.question: Why do saturated hydrocarbons mostly undergo substitution reactions rather than addition reactions?
items.answer: SATURATED hydrocarbons have only SINGLE bonds and are fairly UNREACTIVE (inert) in the presence of most reagents. Since they have no double or triple bonds to add to, they cannot easily undergo addition reactions. Instead, in sunlight, chlorine REPLACES their hydrogen atoms one by one - a substitution reaction.

items.question: Describe the substitution reaction of methane with chlorine and state the role of sunlight.
items.answer:
In the presence of SUNLIGHT, chlorine reacts very FAST with methane (a saturated hydrocarbon). Chlorine REPLACES the hydrogen atoms of methane one by one. The reaction is: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl (in sunlight). SUNLIGHT provides the energy needed to start this fast reaction. With higher homologues of alkanes, a number of substitution products are usually formed.

topics.topic_name: SOME IMPORTANT CARBON COMPOUNDS - ETHANOL AND ETHANOIC ACID

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: DEFINITION: ETHANOL (CH3CH2OH) and ETHANOIC ACID (CH3COOH) are two commercially important carbon compounds. Ethanol is commonly called alcohol and ethanoic acid is commonly called acetic acid.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Many carbon compounds are invaluable to us.
The two commercially important compounds studied here are ETHANOL and ETHANOIC ACID.

items.question: Write the common names and formulae of ethanol and ethanoic acid.
items.answer: ETHANOL (CH3CH2OH) is commonly called alcohol. ETHANOIC ACID (CH3COOH) is commonly called acetic acid.

items.question: What is denatured alcohol?
items.answer: DENATURED ALCOHOL is ethanol made unfit for drinking by adding poisonous substances like methanol, often with a blue dye added for identification, to prevent the misuse of industrial ethanol.

items.question: What is esterification? Write the general reaction.
items.answer: ESTERIFICATION is the reaction in which an ester is formed from an acid and an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst. Reaction: CH3COOH (ethanoic acid) + CH3CH2OH (ethanol) --(acid)--> ester + H2O. Esters are sweet-smelling substances.

items.question: How is ethanol harmful to living beings?
items.answer: When large quantities of ETHANOL are consumed, it slows metabolic processes and depresses the central nervous system, causing lack of coordination, mental confusion, drowsiness, lowering of inhibitions, and finally stupor; judgement and muscular coordination are impaired. Intake of even a small quantity of pure (absolute) ethanol can be lethal, and long-term consumption leads to many health problems.

items.question: Why is the intake of methanol dangerous?
items.answer: Unlike ethanol, intake of METHANOL in very small quantities can cause DEATH. Methanol is oxidised to METHANAL in the liver. Methanal reacts rapidly with the components of cells - it COAGULATES the protoplasm (much as an egg is coagulated by cooking). Methanol also affects the OPTIC NERVE, causing BLINDNESS.

items.question: Describe the reactions of ethanol with sodium and with hot concentrated sulphuric acid.
items.answer:
(i) REACTION WITH SODIUM: Ethanol reacts with sodium, leading to the evolution of hydrogen gas. The other product is sodium ethoxide.
2Na + 2CH3CH2OH -> 2CH3CH2O-Na+ (sodium ethoxide) + H2
(Alcohols react with sodium to produce hydrogen, like some other substances do with metals.)
(ii) REACTION TO GIVE UNSATURATED HYDROCARBON (DEHYDRATION): Heating ethanol at 443 K with excess concentrated sulphuric acid results in the dehydration of ethanol to give ETHENE.
CH3-CH2OH --(Hot conc. H2SO4)--> CH2 = CH2 + H2O
The concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a DEHYDRATING agent which removes water from ethanol.

items.explanation: Ethanol is commonly called alcohol. Acetic acid is ethanoic acid; vinegar is dilute acetic acid.

items.explanation: Ethanoic acid is commonly called acetic acid. Alcohol is ethanol.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Ethanol is a LIQUID at room temperature (see Table 4.1 for its melting and boiling points).
It is commonly called ALCOHOL and is the active ingredient of all alcoholic drinks.
It is a good SOLVENT, used in medicines such as tincture iodine, cough syrups and many tonics.
Ethanol is SOLUBLE in water in all proportions.
Consumption of small quantities of dilute ethanol causes drunkenness; intake of even a small quantity of PURE (absolute) ethanol can be LETHAL; long-term consumption causes many health problems.
REACTIONS OF ETHANOL:
(i) REACTION WITH SODIUM: 2Na + 2CH3CH2OH -> 2CH3CH2O-Na+ (sodium ethoxide) + H2. Alcohols react with sodium leading to the evolution of hydrogen.
(ii) REACTION TO GIVE UNSATURATED HYDROCARBON (dehydration): Heating ethanol at 443 K with excess concentrated sulphuric acid dehydrates it to ethene.
CH3-CH2OH --(Hot conc. H2SO4)--> CH2 = CH2 + H2O. The concentrated sulphuric acid is a dehydrating agent which removes water from ethanol.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (Do you know? - How do alcohols affect living beings?):
sections.text:
- When large quantities of ethanol are consumed, it slows metabolic processes and depresses the central nervous system, causing lack of coordination, mental confusion, drowsiness, lowering of normal inhibitions, and finally stupor; judgement and muscular coordination are seriously impaired.
- Unlike ethanol, intake of METHANOL in very small quantities can cause death. Methanol is oxidised to METHANAL in the liver; methanal reacts rapidly with cell components, coagulating the protoplasm (as an egg is coagulated by cooking). Methanol also affects the OPTIC NERVE, causing BLINDNESS.
- Ethanol is an important industrial solvent. To prevent misuse of industrial ethanol, it is made unfit for drinking by adding poisonous substances like methanol, and blue dyes are added so it can be identified. This is called DENATURED ALCOHOL.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (More to Know - Alcohol as a fuel):
sections.text:
- Sugarcane plants are among the most efficient convertors of sunlight into chemical energy.
- Sugarcane juice can be used to prepare molasses, which is fermented to give alcohol (ethanol).
- Some countries now use alcohol as an additive in petrol since it is a cleaner fuel, giving rise to only carbon dioxide and water on burning in sufficient air (oxygen).

items.question: State two uses of ethanol.
items.answer: Ethanol is used as a good SOLVENT in medicines such as tincture iodine, cough syrups and tonics; it is also the active ingredient of all alcoholic drinks. (It is also used as a cleaner fuel additive in petrol.)

items.question: Write the equation for the reaction of ethanol with sodium.
items.answer: 2Na + 2CH3CH2OH -> 2CH3CH2O-Na+ (sodium ethoxide) + H2. Hydrogen gas is evolved.

items.question: What is the dehydration of ethanol? Write the reaction and name the dehydrating agent.
items.answer: DEHYDRATION of ethanol is the removal of water from ethanol to form an unsaturated hydrocarbon (ethene). Reaction: CH3-CH2OH --(Hot conc. H2SO4, 443 K)--> CH2 = CH2 + H2O. The dehydrating agent is HOT CONCENTRATED SULPHURIC ACID, which removes water from ethanol.

items.question: Describe Activity 4.6 (reaction of ethanol with sodium) and how the gas evolved is tested.
items.answer: A small piece of sodium (about the size of a couple of grains of rice) is dropped into absolute ethanol. A gas is evolved as the sodium reacts with ethanol. The gas is tested by bringing a burning splint near it - it burns with a characteristic "POP" sound, confirming the gas is HYDROGEN. The reaction also forms sodium ethoxide: 2Na + 2CH3CH2OH -> 2CH3CH2O-Na+ + H2.

items.question: Why is industrial alcohol denatured, and how is it done?
items.answer: Ethanol is an important industrial SOLVENT. To prevent the MISUSE of ethanol produced for industrial use (so that it is not consumed as a drink), it is made UNFIT for drinking by adding poisonous substances like METHANOL. Dyes are also added to colour the alcohol BLUE so that it can be identified easily. Alcohol made unfit for drinking in this way is called DENATURED ALCOHOL.

items.question: Explain the physical properties of ethanol and its harmful effects on living beings.
items.answer:
PHYSICAL PROPERTIES: Ethanol is a LIQUID at room temperature, commonly called alcohol. It is a good SOLVENT and is used in medicines like tincture iodine, cough syrups and tonics. It is SOLUBLE in water in all proportions and is the active ingredient of all alcoholic drinks.
HARMFUL EFFECTS: Consumption of small quantities of dilute ethanol causes drunkenness. When large quantities are consumed, ethanol slows metabolic processes and depresses the central nervous system, causing lack of coordination, mental confusion, drowsiness and stupor. Intake of even a small quantity of PURE (absolute) ethanol can be LETHAL, and long-term consumption leads to many health problems. (Methanol is even more dangerous - small quantities can cause death and blindness.)

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Ethanoic acid is commonly called ACETIC ACID and belongs to the group of acids called CARBOXYLIC ACIDS.
A 5-8% solution of acetic acid in water is called VINEGAR, used widely as a preservative in pickles.
The melting point of pure ethanoic acid is 290 K, so it often freezes during winter in cold climates - hence the name GLACIAL ACETIC ACID.
Unlike mineral acids (like HCl) which are completely ionised, carboxylic acids are WEAK acids (only partly ionised).
REACTIONS OF ETHANOIC ACID:
(i) ESTERIFICATION REACTION: Esters are formed by the reaction of an acid and an alcohol. Ethanoic acid reacts with absolute ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst to give an ester:
CH3-COOH (ethanoic acid) + CH3-CH2OH (ethanol) --(acid)--> CH3-CO-O-CH2-CH3 (ester) + H2O.

Esters are sweet-smelling substances used in making perfumes and as flavouring agents. On treating with sodium hydroxide (an alkali), the ester is converted back to alcohol and the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid - this reaction is SAPONIFICATION (used in soap preparation): CH3COOC2H5 --(NaOH)--> C2H5OH + CH3COONa.
(ii) REACTION WITH A BASE: Like mineral acids, ethanoic acid reacts with a base such as sodium hydroxide to give a salt (sodium ethanoate / sodium acetate) and water:
NaOH + CH3COOH -> CH3COONa + H2O.
(iii) REACTION WITH CARBONATES AND HYDROGENCARBONATES: Ethanoic acid reacts with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to give a salt (sodium acetate), carbon dioxide and water:
2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 -> 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2
CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + H2O + CO2

sections.label: ACTIVITY 4.7:
sections.aim: To compare the strength (pH) of dilute acetic acid and dilute hydrochloric acid.
sections.materials: Dilute acetic acid, dilute hydrochloric acid, litmus paper, universal indicator.
procedure: 1. Compare the pH of dilute acetic acid and dilute hydrochloric acid using both litmus paper and universal indicator.
2. Check whether both acids are indicated by the litmus test.
3. Check whether the universal indicator shows them as equally strong acids.

sections.aim: To prepare an ester from ethanol and acetic acid and observe its smell.
sections.materials: 1 mL ethanol (absolute alcohol), 1 mL glacial acetic acid, concentrated sulphuric acid (a few drops), test tube, water bath, beaker with 20-50 mL water.
procedure: 1. Take 1 mL ethanol (absolute alcohol) and 1 mL glacial acetic acid along with a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid in a test tube.

3. Pour into a beaker containing 20-50 mL of water and smell the resulting mixture.

sections.conclusion: Ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid (acid catalyst) to form a sweet-smelling ESTER. This is the ESTERIFICATION reaction.

sections.aim: To study the reaction of ethanoic acid with sodium carbonate and sodium hydrogencarbonate.

procedure: 1. Set up the apparatus as shown in Chapter 2, Activity 2.5.
2. Take a spatula full of sodium carbonate in a test tube and add 2 mL of dilute ethanoic acid.
3. Observe what happens.
4. Pass the gas produced through freshly prepared lime-water and observe.
5. Repeat the activity with sodium hydrogencarbonate instead of sodium carbonate.
sections.observation: Brisk EFFERVESCENCE is seen (a gas is produced). The gas turns lime-water MILKY, showing it is CARBON DIOXIDE.
sections.conclusion:
Ethanoic acid reacts with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to give a salt (commonly sodium acetate), carbon dioxide and water:
2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 -> 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2
CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + H2O + CO2

items.question: What is vinegar? Why is ethanoic acid called glacial acetic acid?
items.answer: VINEGAR is a 5-8% solution of acetic acid in water, used widely as a preservative in pickles. Pure ethanoic acid has a melting point of 290 K, so it freezes (forms ice-like crystals) during winter in cold climates - hence it is called GLACIAL ACETIC ACID.

items.question: Write the reaction of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide.
items.answer: NaOH + CH3COOH -> CH3COONa (sodium ethanoate/acetate) + H2O. Ethanoic acid reacts with the base to give a salt and water.

items.question: What is esterification? What is saponification?
items.answer: ESTERIFICATION is the reaction in which an ester (sweet-smelling) is formed from an acid and an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst: CH3COOH + C2H5OH --(acid)--> ester + H2O. SAPONIFICATION is the reverse reaction in which the ester, on treatment with sodium hydroxide (alkali), is converted back to alcohol and the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid; it is used in the preparation of SOAP.

items.question: Describe Activity 4.9 (reaction of ethanoic acid with carbonates/hydrogencarbonates) and the test for the gas.
items.answer:
A spatula full of sodium carbonate is taken in a test tube and 2 mL of dilute ethanoic acid is added. Brisk EFFERVESCENCE occurs as a gas is released. The gas is passed through freshly prepared LIME-WATER, which turns MILKY, confirming the gas is CARBON DIOXIDE. The same is repeated with sodium hydrogencarbonate. Reactions:
2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 -> 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2
CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + H2O + CO2

items.question: Why is ethanoic acid called a weak acid? How is this shown in Activity 4.7?
items.answer: Ethanoic acid is a CARBOXYLIC acid. Unlike mineral acids (such as HCl) which are COMPLETELY ionised, carboxylic acids are only PARTLY ionised, so they are WEAK acids. In Activity 4.7, both dilute acetic acid and dilute HCl turn blue litmus red (both are acids), but the UNIVERSAL INDICATOR shows acetic acid as a weaker acid (different pH) than hydrochloric acid - showing they are NOT equally strong.

items.question: Describe the esterification reaction of ethanoic acid (Activity 4.8), the properties of esters, and saponification.
items.answer:
ESTERIFICATION (Activity 4.8): 1 mL ethanol and 1 mL glacial acetic acid with a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid are taken in a test tube and warmed in a water bath for at least five minutes, then poured into water and smelt. A SWEET-SMELLING ester is formed:
CH3COOH + C2H5OH --(acid)--> CH3-CO-O-C2H5 (ester) + H2O.
PROPERTIES OF ESTERS: Esters are SWEET-SMELLING substances, used in making perfumes and as flavouring agents.
SAPONIFICATION: On treating the ester with sodium hydroxide (an alkali), it is converted back to alcohol and the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid. This reaction is called SAPONIFICATION because it is used in the preparation of SOAP. Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids.

items.explanation: This reverse reaction is saponification, used in soap preparation.

items.explanation: Pure acetic acid freezes (melting point 290 K) in cold winters, forming ice-like crystals, hence "glacial".

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Most dirt is OILY in nature, and oil does not dissolve in water.
Soap molecules are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids.
A soap molecule has two ends with differing properties:
One end is HYDROPHILIC (ionic end) - interacts with WATER.
The other end is HYDROPHOBIC (carbon chain) - interacts with OIL.

MICELLE: When soap is in water, the molecules form clusters called micelles - the hydrophobic (carbon) tails point towards the oil droplet (interior) and the hydrophilic (ionic) ends face outside (towards water). This forms an EMULSION in water.
The soap micelle helps pull out the dirt; the oily dirt is collected in the centre of the micelle and rinsed away.
Micelles stay in solution as a COLLOID and do not precipitate due to ion-ion repulsion. Soap micelles are large enough to SCATTER light, so a soap solution appears CLOUDY.
In a hydrocarbon (non-aqueous) solvent, the orientation would be reversed (ionic ends inside).
HARD WATER contains calcium and magnesium salts. Soap reacts with these to form an insoluble substance called SCUM, so more soap is needed and foam forms with difficulty.

DETERGENTS are generally sodium salts of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts with chlorides/bromides, with long hydrocarbon chains. Their charged ends do NOT form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions in hard water, so they remain effective in hard water.
Detergents are usually used to make shampoos and products for cleaning clothes.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 4.10:
sections.aim: To study the effect of soap on the mixing of oil and water.
sections.materials: Two test tubes, water, cooking oil, soap solution.
procedure: 1. Take about 10 mL of water each in two test tubes.
2. Add a drop of oil (cooking oil) to both test tubes and label them A and B.
3. To test tube B, add a few drops of soap solution.
4. Shake both test tubes vigorously for the same period of time.
5. Check if the oil and water layers separate immediately after shaking.
6. Leave the test tubes undisturbed for some time and observe in which test tube the oil layer separates out first.
sections.observation: In test tube A (no soap), the oil and water separate quickly. In test tube B (with soap), the oil and water do not separate easily - an emulsion forms and the oil layer separates out later (or not at all soon).
sections.conclusion: Soap helps oil and water to mix by forming micelles/emulsion, which is the basis of its cleaning action. Without soap, oil and water separate quickly.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 4.11:
sections.aim: To compare the foaming of soap in soft (distilled/rain) water and hard water.
sections.materials: Distilled water (or rain water), hard water (from a tubewell/hand-pump), soap solution, test tubes. (Note for teacher: if hard water is not available, prepare it by dissolving hydrogencarbonates/sulphates/chlorides of calcium or magnesium in water.)
procedure: 1. Take about 10 mL of distilled water (or rain water) and 10 mL of hard water in separate test tubes.
2. Add a couple of drops of soap solution to both.
3. Shake the test tubes vigorously for an equal period of time and observe the amount of foam formed.
4. Note in which test tube more foam forms and in which a white curdy precipitate forms.
sections.observation: More FOAM forms in the distilled/rain (soft) water. In the hard water, a white CURDY PRECIPITATE (scum) forms and less foam is produced.
sections.conclusion: Soap forms a white curdy precipitate (scum) with the calcium and magnesium salts of hard water, so it lathers (foams) poorly in hard water but well in soft water.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 4.12:
sections.aim: To compare the behaviour of soap and detergent in hard water.
sections.materials: Two test tubes, hard water, soap solution, detergent solution.
procedure: 1. Take two test tubes with about 10 mL of hard water in each.
2. Add five drops of soap solution to one and five drops of detergent solution to the other.
3. Shake both test tubes for the same period.
4. Check if both have the same amount of foam.
5. Check in which test tube a curdy solid is formed.
sections.observation: The detergent forms MORE foam in hard water and does NOT form a curdy precipitate, whereas the soap forms less foam and a curdy solid (scum).
sections.conclusion: Detergents remain effective in hard water (they do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions), while soap does not work well in hard water (forms scum). Hence detergents are used to make shampoos and cleaning products.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (More to Know - Micelles):
sections.text:
- Soaps are molecules in which the two ends have differing properties - one is HYDROPHILIC (interacts with water) and the other is HYDROPHOBIC (interacts with hydrocarbons / does not dissolve in water).
- When soap is at the surface of water, the hydrophobic 'tail' is not soluble in water, so the soap aligns along the water surface with the ionic end in water and the hydrocarbon 'tail' protruding out of the water.
- Inside water, these molecules form a unique orientation that keeps the hydrocarbon portion out of the water - clusters called MICELLES, with hydrocarbon tails in the interior and ionic ends on the surface.
- Soap in a micelle is able to clean since the oily dirt is collected in the centre of the micelle.
- Micelles stay in solution as a COLLOID and do not come together to precipitate because of ION-ION repulsion. The dirt suspended in micelles is easily rinsed away.
- Soap micelles are large enough to SCATTER light, so a soap solution appears CLOUDY.

items.question: What are soaps chemically? Why do most dirt require soap to be removed?
items.answer: Soaps are SODIUM or POTASSIUM salts of long-chain CARBOXYLIC ACIDS. Most dirt is OILY in nature and oil does not dissolve in water, so soap is needed to remove it by forming micelles/emulsions.

items.question: What is a micelle?
items.answer: A MICELLE is a cluster of soap molecules formed in water in which the hydrophobic (carbon) tails point towards the interior (oil droplet) and the hydrophilic (ionic) ends face outward towards the water, forming an emulsion that traps oily dirt.

items.question: Why does a soap solution appear cloudy?
items.answer: In water, soap molecules form clusters called MICELLES. These micelles stay in solution as a COLLOID (do not precipitate, due to ion-ion repulsion). Soap micelles are LARGE enough to SCATTER light, and this scattering of light makes the soap solution appear CLOUDY.

items.question: Explain the cleaning action of soap using the structure of a soap molecule.
items.answer: A soap molecule has two ends: a HYDROPHILIC (ionic) end that interacts with water and a HYDROPHOBIC (carbon chain) end that interacts with oil. When soap is added to water with oily dirt, the hydrophobic tails attach to the oil droplet and the hydrophilic ends face the water, forming a MICELLE. The oily dirt is trapped in the centre of the micelle, forming an emulsion. The micelles stay suspended in water (colloid) and the dirt is easily RINSED away with water, cleaning the surface.

items.question: Why does soap not work well in hard water, while detergents do?
items.answer: HARD WATER contains calcium and magnesium salts. Soap reacts with these to form an insoluble white substance (SCUM), so a larger amount of soap is needed and it lathers poorly. DETERGENTS are sodium salts of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts with long hydrocarbon chains; their charged ends do NOT form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions in hard water. Hence detergents remain effective in hard water, while soap does not.

items.question: Describe the structure of a soap molecule, the formation of a micelle, and how it removes oily dirt.
items.answer:
STRUCTURE: A soap molecule (sodium/potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid) has two ends with different properties - a HYDROPHILIC ionic end (interacts with water) and a HYDROPHOBIC carbon-chain tail (interacts with oil, does not dissolve in water).
MICELLE FORMATION: In water, the hydrophobic tails cannot stay in water, so the molecules arrange into clusters called MICELLES - the hydrocarbon tails point inward (towards the interior/oil) and the ionic ends point outward into the water.
REMOVAL OF DIRT: Oily dirt is collected in the CENTRE of the micelle, forming an EMULSION. The micelles stay suspended in water as a colloid (do not precipitate, due to ion-ion repulsion). When the cloth is rinsed, the dirt trapped in the micelles is washed away, cleaning the cloth. Micelles scatter light, so soap solution looks cloudy.
